Fumigating stations, $3,000.
Although the amount of this item is small, it is still very important and the committee should have full information.

I am ready to give as full information as I can. The hon. gentleman is aware of the origin of this work. Some years ago parliament passed a law prohibiting the importation of any nursery stock from any country where the San Jose scale was known. This prohibition lasted for about two years without relaxation, and an amendment was then passed by which nursery stock was permitted to be imported at certain ports of entry designated by Order in Council on the condition that it should be carefully fumigated. This sum is for the carrying out of that law. Nursery stock is allowed by the Order in Council passed under that Act, to come in during a certain season of the year at St. John, N.B., St. Johns, P.Q., Niagara Palls and Windsor, Ont., Winnipeg, Man.,and Vancouver, B.C. At each of these ports there is a small building made as nearly air tight as possible and a man is employed there during certain months of the year who takes the stock from the customs, puts it in the air chamber, fumigates it with hydrocyanic acid and then sends it back to customs. This has been carried on for two seasons and has been found to work on the whole very satisfactorily. There have been many requests that tlie period for importation should be lengthened, but the Order in Council was drawn up on the advice of the experts of my department, and I believe that the time is sufficiently long for people who pay attention to their work to import what they find necessary. The relaxation of the original San Jose Act was due to the request of growers of trees and shrubs in this country to enable them to import certain varieties, in some instances which they could not get in this country. It was also due to their demand that they would be allowed to have some cheek, so to speak, on the growers of nursery stock in this country 12
who at that time were hardly able to meet the market demand.

The hon. gentleman will-see from his experience that good came of the necessity. It has been the means of largely increasing the growth of nursery stock in Canada. Whether or not that stock is entirely free fropi the San Jose scale is yet an open question. It has no doubt come to the notice of the hon. gentleman that there is a murmur throughout the country that either from imperfect examination at the fumigation station, or from the rapid spread of the insect in Canada, it is becoming more dangerous all the time, to such an extent that in some directions people are somewhat discouraged at the prospect. I fully approve of the measures that were taken with regard to nursery stock imported into Canada; but there is the greater question as to how we are to deal with the insect as it is now planted on Canadian soil. The hon. gentleman and the Ontario government made some efforts to stamp it out, either working together or working separately, I am not prepared to say ; and some orchards were cut down in the face of almost open rebellion against the conduct of the two governments. It seems, however, that the whole matter has come to a standstill. I am told, although I am not prepared to vouch for the correctness of the statement, that forest trees are becoming infected with the insect. I believe it was stated at one of the meetings of the Agricultural Committee last year, that that was not the case ; but I have made some inquiries since, and I am told that many forest trees have become infected with this insect. If that is true, it becomes a very serious matter, and I am sure nothing would be more welcome to the committee than to have some intimation from the hon. gentleman as to what his policy is for dealing with this very important matter in the future.

I am very glad to meet the hon. gentleman's wishes. First, I would like to say, not in connection but in amplification of'what he has said, that while the Ontario goverry ment has done something towards stamping out the scale in the province of Ontario, tliis government and my department have had nothing whatever to do with that part of the work, which has been entirely under the control of the provincial authorities and their officers. The work which we have done in my department lias been two fold [DOT] First, by means of the San Jose Scale Act, to prevent the importation of the scale into this country from abroad-that was the object of this vote ; and. secondly, by means of the officers of the Experimental Farm-through Mr. Saunders, the head of that establishment, who is himself a horticulturist, a botanist and an entomologist ; through Mr. Fletcher, who is the entom'-l-ogist and botanist of the farm, and through



Mr. Macoun, who Is the' horticulturist of the farm we have been spreading information amkmg the fruit-growers and tree-growers of the country in regard to the dangers of the San Jose scale and the best treatment for exterminating or checking it. That has been the work of my department. Now, I think I may safely say that there is hardly any San Jose scale, if any at all, in any part of the Dominion of Canada except in the province of Ontario. It is barely possible that there may be a little in the province of British Columbia, hut the people there say that it has been entirely stamped out, and I am disposed to believe them. We are not aware of a single instance in the province of Quebec or in the maritime provinces. In the province of Ontario the provincial authorities have passed laws and issued regulations which have been fairly effective. They have been trying to stamp out the disease in some instances by cutting down the trees and burning them, and in other instances by elaborate methods of fumigation. They have been checking it by the regulation that all nursery stock grown in the province of Ontario must be fumigated by hydrocyanic acid gas before being issued from the nursery. If the fumigation is properly conducted-and the report of the officers is that it is-it effectually kills any scale that may exist on nursery stock ; and I think I am safe in saying, what I have stated frequently-and I have been supported and corroborated by experts, that the San Jose scale is not being spread by nursery stock grown in the province of Ontario. I do not believe that the stock sent out from the province of Ontario can carry the scale after the treatment it universally receives before it is issued. The scale does spread most wonderfully by the ordinary means of spreading disease or insect life, and in days gone by it has spread soihewhat considerably in certain parts in the province of Ontario, but only in that province. I am happy to understand, from the reports of those who have been inspecting it of late, that the methods of fighting the scale have been very much improved, and that if the proprietors of orchards and forest trees and shrubs choose to carry out properly and effectively the instructions given to them by the entomologists and botanists, they can destroy it. Unfortunately, however, these gentlemen are human, like' the rest of us, and a great many do not attend to their work properly, while others do not attend to it at all. So that occasionally no doubt the scale will get on forest trees. If this kind of thing goes on, the scale will perhaps increase in certain parts ; but any one who chooses to carry out the instructions given by experts on the subject can stamp it out and keep his orchards and small fruits free of it.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will remember that Professor Fletcher
Hon. Mr. FISHER
stated that there were two methods of meeting the difficulty. One was to use certain solutions on the trees, and the other was to fumigate with hydrocyanic acid gas. The latter method, however, was said to be so expensive although the really effectual method of destroying the insect that it would not be generally adopted. Therefore, the milder and less effective method was being pursued, and while it served as a sort of check, there was no assurance that it was stamping out the disease.	-

The treatment by hydrocyanic acid is very difficult in the case of large trees and very expensive. The cost and the trouble makes it almost prohibitory. That method is used in fumigating nursery stock and small bushes, which can be easily covered and effectively fumigated.
Where is the nursery stock fumigated ?

It is only fumigated in Ontario. There is none grown anywhere else where we are aware of any scale being in existence. That work is done by the nursery men at their own nurseries under the inspection of an officer of the Ontario government. The fumigation stations only deal with importations and have nothing to do with nursery stock grown in this country. As regards the methods of destroying the scale, the fumigation by hydrocyanic acid gas of large trees is a very difficult, expensive and troublesome operation, and, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred would probably not be effective. But no doubt the hydrocyanic gas is absolute death to the scale wherever the scale is touched by it. The ordinary method of spraying petroleum or whale oil is much more easy and cheaper and can be applied by anybody. It is not as effective as fumigation but is none the less a very effective method of dealing with the scale. While in one treatment all the scales might not be destroyed, any one who would take the trouble to spray the trees several times will effectively destroy them.

It seems to me when these gentlemen are allowed such liberal expenses as $5 and $6 per day, they can pay petty tips out of their own pockets. It may of course appear light to the minister that these men should travel in this style, but to the ordinary taxpayer it must be a_ matter of comment that, allowing them $5 and $G a day, they are still permitted to indulge in all these extravagances. No doubt as one of these gentlemen was to have charge of the expenditure everything went according to his taste. I hope that when Mr. Brodie goes to Wolverhampton, as the minister states he will, he will not ask the country to pay for one or two travelling bags for himself.

I am afraid the expense of transfer from one place to another would be a good deal more than the buildings are worth. When they were built the St. Louis Fair was not even started. I may mention here that I have been authorized by council to accept the invitation which has been extended by the authorities of St. Louis to Canada to participate in that exhibition, which will take place in 1903.

From the appearance of the Canadian building at Buffalo the country will not be astonished to learn that it did not bring much. I have no hesitation in saying, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian building was a perfect disgrace to Canada.
Oh.

I appreciate the hon. gentleman's difficulty in securing a location.

He was much in the hands of the authorities there, and perhaps could not help himself. 1 am not disposed to find fault with that, although it is a regrettable matter that the building was not better located. But those who attended that exhibition could not help but be impressed with the poor appearance of the Canadian building. The smallest state in the union had a more presentable building than we had. I think there is nothing more damaging than to be beggarly, if that was the reason of it. When Canada was taking part in an exhibition of the continent of America, it should not have been behind any state in the union. If we could afford to expend any sum of money in the interest of Canada we should at least have expended enough to make a respectable appearance. Why, Sir, that building looked more like a barn than anything else. I could find horse stables in Canada that had a better appearance. It was not so bad inside, but outside the appearance of that building must have stamped Canadians as a set of people a generation behind the times. Now, I repudiate any idea of that kind. But I think it is not creditable to the management of the hon. gentleman that he permitted a building for Canadian exhibitors to be shown to the whole world as the most shabby building upon the whole ground. There were buildings not so large by some of the states, but they were all tastefully got up, they were presentable. While I think that great care should always be taken in the expenditure of public money, I know nothing of greater importance on such occasions than to present an appearance in keeping with our position. I think we have lost reputation in consequence of that building, if we did not redeem ourselves by other means, namely, by our splendid exhibits that came from all the provinces, and particularly from Ontario, and which gave all Canadians a very laudable pride. But the disgraceful part of it was the shabby appearance of the Canadian building.

I take exception to the remarks of the hon. member for Both-well (Mr. Clancy). I think the building was a credit to Canada. I had the pleasure of attending the Pan-American twice. I went through that building, and I am satisfied that there was no building on the ground more creditable than that building was to Canada. The way it was fitted up inside and the display that was made in it, was something grand, and every man I-spoke to was proud to think that Canada made such a showing.

I confess I have not that practised eye for architectural beauty that my hon. friend has who lives on the back concessions. I will venture to say that there is not an intelligent man in Canada who will support his opinion. I call upon the
Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) an experienced judge.
I am not a judge.

No, but I have no hesitation in saying that the Minister of Public Works would not be prepared to say that if Canada made an exhibit there at all it included the building as well as the contents, and the building ought to be of high order. My hon. friend knows that it had a shingled roof on it, without paint, as other buildings had, and when the hon. gentleman says that it was a credit to Canada, then we will have to ascribe that entirely to his exalted taste, which is at variance with that of every half-cultured gentleman in this country.

I fear that I must set myself down as having no intelligence, in the opinion of the hon. gentleman. But I was very much surprised at his strictures upon the Canadian building at Buffalo. I myself have heard very many encomiums made on the style of architecture and the suitability of the building for such purpose. It is true it had a shingle roof, but I think that if the hon. gentleman will examine a great many of the other buildings at Buffalo he will find that they have shingle roofs, too. If he will examine many of the most beautiful and artistic buildings of the present day he will find that they have shingle roofs. The hon. gentleman has spoken of the situation of the building in the Buffalo grounds.
I did not criticise that.

The hon. gentleman has not criticized that, but I want to point out to him that the situation was for business purposes an extremely good one. The situation was near the exhibits at the exhibition buildings and especially near to where the agricultural exhibits, in which Canada was most largely engaged, were placed. The other state buildings, which the hon. gentleman "has compared with it, were placed away at an outside corner of the grounds, a place which would have been extremely inconvenient for Canadian visitors or exhibitors to make their rendezvous or headquarters. As a matter of fact at the end of the PanAmerican exhibition there was a gathering of the different state commissioners and they severely took to task the exhibition authorities for having placed their state buildings in such an unsatisfactory situation. They instanced the situation of the Canadian building as being so superior to that in which the state buildings were placed and said that it was an unfair advantage which had been given to Canada, an unfair advantage due to my own insistence that the Canadian building should not be placed among the state buildings.
Tlie lion, gentleman was wise In not putting it among the state buildings.
Who is H. C. Bride, the architect ? Is he an American or a Canadian architect ?
He is an architect, of London, Ont.
I see that he received $1,300 in fees. What was the total of the fees he received for his work in connection with that building ?

I cannot, off-hand, say what the total would he. I will give you the total when I come down with the supplementary vote. Mr. Bride got the usual architectural fees with the addition of some travelling expenses for having to go to Buffalo and spend some time there arranging the contracts for the building.

Mr. Chairman, I do not pretend to be a critic of the building; in fact, it was scarcely completed when I saw it. My attention was drawn more to the character of what I saw inside. I thought that if the furniture in that building was intended to be an exhibit of Canadian furniture, it should have bpen of a higher order. I think I mentioned this to the gentleman in charge at the time. I thought it was a grand opportunity to make a first-class exhibit of Canadian woods and furniture. I do not know whether the furniture was made there or whether it was made In Canada, but it did not come up to the mark of what I thought should have been found in the Canadian building.

The furniture was not intended to be used as an exhibit, but it was supplied by the company, which, I believe, is a consolidation of the furniture^ Jnanufaeturers of Ontario. I forget the exact name, but I think it is the Canada Furniture Manufacturing Company. They asked to be allowed to furnish that building free of charge to the government and they put in what they considered to be their very best exhibit.
I do not think it was.

I am not responsible for it. They had a free hand, and they did what they thought to their own interest. I must confess that 1 thought, myself, while visiting it, that it was very handsome furniture. At the end of the exhibition there was some slight damage to some of it and the commissioner recommended that we should pay them a small indemnity for that damage-I think $250. That is all the government had to pay for the use of all the furniture in the building.

For renewing and improving Canadian exhibit at Imperial Institute, London, $3,000.

This is a matter that has invited discussion in the past. It has been stated in this House that the Imperial Institute, as far as it was educational in Great Britain, was a failure. The hon. gentleman is asking for the same sum this year that he had last. I am not urging an increase of the expenditure, but I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me tiiai if we had an exhibition of that kind in Great Britain which is ever to serve some useful purpose, it ought to accomplish that end to some extent. Those who have visited Great Britain tell me, because, personally I have no knowledge of it whatever, that it is not in the right place, that it is a back number if one may be permitted to use such a slang, and-^I think we had a promise from the hon. minister last year, as well as, I think, from the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that something would be done to make that expenditure although a very small one, somewhat effective, either by increasing it or in some other way.

Before the hon. minister rises to speak possibly oue answer will serve for two questions. I understand that the Imperial Institute so far as it is being utilized for the purpose for which it has hitherto existed and was designed has been closed and that the materials have been moved to some other part of the city of London.

In reply, first to tlie lion, member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes), I would say that the Imperial Institute just now is in a transition stage and has been within the last few months. It has been an entirely independent organization under a commissioner, or a president-I think he is called- and a board appointed by various authorities in the old country. Lately there have been several meetings at which it is apparent to me, having had reports of those meetings both from Lord Strathcona and through the press, that the Imperial Institute has been handed over to the Imperial Board of Trade, one of the departments of tlie Imperial government. So far I have not been able to find out exactly what that department intends to do. The representative of Canada at the Imperial Institute, Mr. Watson, has written to me several times and he informs me that, as far as he can gather, not having entire information from the authorities, that the work and objects of the Institute will be continued very much on the same lines, but under different authority and control. The exhibits are still in the same building and they are to be continued there as far as I can obtain any information, but it is in a transition stage. In regard to the exhibits there, I would first like to point out to the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) and the committee that the exhibits have not been under the control of this parliament. They have been supplied by the various provincial governments, and it has been the provincial governments which have managed them, looked after them, repaired them and kept them in order. At the time of the Paris Exhibition, when we had a very extensive collection of mineral exhibits from Canada and very considerable forestry and other exhibits, I was urged by Lord Strathcona and those interested in the Imperial Institute to place them in the Imperial Institute. When I was in England I visited the Institute, and I found the conditions much as the hon. gentleman has described. Our exhibits there are not a credit to Canada in their numbers or their character, or in the condition they are in. Many of them are very old, and should be replaced, while others ought to be repaired. In consequence of the opening of the Glasgow exhibition, the Paris exhibits which I intended for the Imperial Institute were sent to Glasgow, and at the present time they are in the exhibit at the Royal Exchange in London. Last autumn various people in London interested in colonial investments decided to have a London exhibition of the colonial exhibits at Glasgow. We were asked to send our exhibits there and after a good deal of discussion and some hitches the exhibit at the Royal Exchange was arranged for, and will be opened on the 1st of March. I was
authorized by my colleagues to do this, and as it was believed that especially the mineral exhibit would be of vast interest to the investing public in London, many who are interested in mining matters in Canada urged strongly that these exhibits should be shown in the financial centre of the world. At the close of the Royal Exchange exhibition, it is the intention to send a large portion of this exhibit to the Imperial Institute if the arraugements in connection with tlie Imperial Institute then admit of it. Some of this vote last year was used in carrying the exhibits to London, and in cleaning them up and repairing them.

If my memory serves me right, the attention of the minister was drawn on a former occasion to the unsatisfactory character of the Canadian exhibits at the Imperial Institute. Did I understand from the hon. gentleman, that the Imperial Institute is not under the same management now as it was formerly ? Are these old exhibits to be permitted to remain or are they to be brought up to date ? Friends of mine who have visited the Imperial Institute have expressed their regret to me that a more creditable Canadian exhibit was not made there. Are any steps being taken to direct the attention of those who placed the exhibits there, to the necessity, in the interest of Canada, of having them renewed ? There is no use spending money to have a second or third-class exhibit, because that does the country harm rather than good.

I have urged on the representatives of tlie provinces whose exhibits these are that they should do something. I confess that there has been an inclination on the part of the provinces to throw that responsibility and expense on us. I have not received any official documents which would bear on this, but the tenor of the replies I have had in conversation is : If you do not think the exhibit good enough, go ahead yourself. I fear that the probability of the provincial governments doing a great deal towards having a good exhibit at the Imperial Institute is, to say the least, doubtful. Of course, I have no authority to interfere with these exhibits, but I hope that when the Royal Exchange exhibition is over, the management of the Imperial Institute will be finally settled upon, and then I will be able to utilize this vote to the best possible advantage. I want to warn hon. gentlemen, that $3,000 will not be sufficient to make a very creditable exhibit at the Imperial Institute, and especially if the provincial authorities are going to drop out I will have to ask for a larger sum.
Has the new emigration building which is to be opened up by this government on the Strand, anything to do with the Department of Agriculture ?
No.

That matter is entirely in charge of the Minister of the Interior. Quarantine-Salaries and contingencies of organized districts and public health in other districts, $110,000.

This is an item which covers the whole quarantine service of my department. It deals with the seaboard quarantine, and this year it deals very largely with the quarantine along the international boundary line between Canada and the United States. The item has assumed much larger proportions recently in consequence of the unfortunate prevalence of small-pox in the United States and the alarm which our people all along the frontier have felt with regard to it. The vote is however the same as it was last year when we had the same difficulty to contend against. It covers the quarantine at Halifax. Charlottetown, St. Johns, Sydney, Grosse Isle at Quebec, Victoria, British Columbia, and also all the unorganized quarantine work done on our seaboard and along the frontier. In addition to this we have recently had to do a good deal in connection with public health in the territories in consequence of the prevalence of small-pox. We have had to take steps to protect that portion of the country which, not being organized into a province, has no provincial authority or organization to deal with public health. We have had to assume that work and will have to continue it for the future until the territories are so organized as to have proper provincial organization.

As the hon. gentleman gave it, they still seem to be in the service. Now, if the reports that come to me arc correct there are others than those the hon. minister has mentioned. I would like to ask him if there is not a medical gentleman by the name of Dr. McCully employed at Rondeau Point, Ontario ?

I was wrong in saying that these were all that have been employed. This, I am informed, is a list of fhose who are still employed. Some have been engaged along the chain of lakes during the summer for short periods at different times. I have not a list of them here.

I think the committee would be interested in hearing the list of those that have been employed, with the

length of service of each and the amount paid. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could give us that ?
I have not that list with me to-night.
Then, the hon. minister had better let the item stand.
The hon. minister did not give the list of the chief officers for Quebec employed along the frontier.

I am glad to say that the United States immediately south of Quebec is in such a healthy state that we have not required to watch the frontier. We have not had to appoint any one in the province of Quebec, and, I believe, with the exception of Cornwall, none in eastern Ontario.
We have had a good deal of small-pox coming into Quebec from the States.

We have no reports to that effect either from the local authorities or frotn anybody who required our action. As a general rule we have taken, in the first place, reports of the United States authorities as to the condition of affairs in the country south of our boundary ; and, in the second place, the request for reports of the provincial health authorities. Where the provincial health authorities have not expressed any fear in regard to the frontier, and where we have reports of satisfactory conditions to the south of the line, we have not appointed any officer.
Has there been a report from the provincial health authorities that there is no small-pox in the New England states ?

No, I did not say that. I said that the provincial health authorities have made no request for us to guard the frontier, and that we have had reports from the United States health authorities as to the condition of health in the different states along the border, and that we took these two sources of information as our guide.
Is there any report as to the state of health in the New England states in the possession of the department ?
The reports of the health authorities of the U nited States are all sent to my department, and my chief superintendent of public health studies these all the time.
I understand there is a report in the department that there is no small-pox to fear in the New England states, no smallpox in existence in the New England states. I would like to see that report.

There is no report showing there is no small-Mr. CLANCY.
pox in the United States. But their reports do say that the health authorities there are handling it and managing it so that there is no likelihood of its spreading.
Can the minister tell us liow these medical men operate to prevent the importation of small-pox ?
They watch passing trains. They go down below the frontier and look at the people on the trains, wherever an officer is appointed.
I understood the minister to say that he does not put an officer on unless lie has information from the American health authorities that there is small-pox on the other side of the line.

Not quite that. We watch the health reports of the United States, all the health reports from all sources in the United States come to our department, and the superintendent of public healtli keeps watch of these, and if the conditions south of the line are not such as to be a menace to our health, we do not appoint any officer; but when in his judgment they menace our safety, then we appoint an officer.
I noticed last season that the disease was imported especially from Michigan. What precautions have been taken to prevent travellers bringing it across the line from that part of the United States ?
We have had officers at the several ports opposite northern Michigan, where boats come from that region, and they watch the travel all the time.
Has the minister under consideration the formation of a Dominion board of health, or would it come under his department ?

I think if any board of health were organized it would come under my department, which now deals especially with that subject. While that question might be discussed, it has hardly reached.a point where I could make a statement.
In case of the importation of the disease by trains or otherwise, has any effort been made to have the health department on the other side bear the expense of looking after this ?

They do it for themselves on their own side of the line, the same as we bear the expense of looking after small-pox on our side of the line. We have not asked them to share the expense of protecting our health.

Is there any small-pox now in that portion of New York state known as the Adirondack Mountains,

through which the Ottawa and New York Railway runs ?
I noticed something of that kind, and therefore put a man on at Cornwall.

What are the reports now in regard to small-pox in that locality ? I understand that there is none, that there is no possibility of any small-pox coming over that line, and that that man is only employed in examining passengers on that railway.
My officer says that the later reports show that there is no danger, and that we may be able to dispense with that man's services.

I want to ask the minister to take better means to protect the people of Prince Edward Island from a smallpox epidemic. The minister has read the names of several doctors who are stationed at ports along the shores, and they are very good men, vigilant and active, who attend to their duties in every respect. But I want to make a remark concerning a case that occurred at Georgetown, in Prince Edward Island, last fall. I do not know if the hon. gentleman who was at the head of the provincial government at the time is in the House; but I know that a man was smitten with small-pox and so declared by the doctor at that port, and he was taken into a carriage and driven from Georgetown to Kep-poch, where there is a marine hospital, a distance of thirty miles, right through the country, exposing the people to the danger of infection all through that section. 1 would ask the hon. gentleman why that was allowed to occur ? Is there any conflict between the two authorities, or why should not both authorities unite to guard the public health in that respect ? I also want to ask the hon. gentleman if all the employees- not speaking of the doctors, who are able to look after themselves-if all the attendants, and the nurses at the marine hospital at Keppoch, have been paid by the government ? Have all the bills in connection with the marine hospital at Charlottetown been paid by this government ? When we are again threatened in Prince Edward Island with an epidemic originating outside of our island, I want to impress upon the hon. gentleman that he should take the greatest care to protect the people of that province. I say it was a shameful thing that this man, declared to have small-pox, should have been driven across the country in a carriage that was not flagged to warn the people that he had small-pox, that he was allowed to talk and chat with the people on the way, and the driver broke his carriage on many occasions, and all these circumstances increased the danger of spreading the contagion. I would ask the minister why it was that that thing occurred ? Whose fault was it ? Was it the
fault of the Dominion government or of the local government ? I would ask the hon. minister to make some statement in connection with the facts and also to say whether these nurses who were employed at the hospital at Charlottetown have been paid as they required.

In reply to the hon. gentleman I would say that I suppose I know by report the case to which he refers. It was the case of a seaman who had been some days in the port of Georgetown before the disease was discovered and the man was no longer subject to our supervision, inspection, or examination. We are responsible on the arrival of the vessel for giving that vessel a clean bill of health. When the vessel receives a clean bill of health from our officers, we have no more responsibility for anything in connection with its crew than we would have in connection with a farmer in the neighbourhood of the town. I am not aware of the details of the case such as the hon. gentleman describes. If anything has been done it has been done in no sense under the authority or control of my department. Such a case would be entirely under the control of the provincial health authorities over whom we have no control and with whom we do not interfere. As far as the hon. gentleman's question about the marine hospital at Charlottetown is concerned, I would say that there is perhaps a little confusion in the name. We have a quarantine hospital there. I do not think there is anything that is called a marine hospital at that place. The marine hospitals are in charge of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). I have no control over them and they are used for a different purpose to that for which the quarantine stations are used. As far as the quarantine station at Charlottetown is concerned, there was one case which was dealt with by my officer there and the doctor and nurses and everybody connected with the ease have been paid. I am informed that at the request of the authorities at Charlottetown, a local case was allowed to be treated at the quarantine hospital, but the local authorities have to deal with it and they have to pay for it. I simply allowed them to utilize the quarantine hospital for the convenience of the city of Charlottetown.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to dispute with the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett), but I wish to say that he has exaggerated the facts in connection with this matter. This man was taken sick at Georgetown, and as the Minister of Agriculture (ITon. Mr. Fisher) states, the marine hospital at Keppoch, near Charlottetown, was used for the reception of the patient. As soon as it was known that the man had smallpox he was driven to the hospital in a closed

carriage. How could he have been taken otherwise Y He could not have been taken on the railway. That would have been a greater danger to the public health. He was driven to the hospital in a closed carriage by a man who had had the smallpox, himself, previously. A bolt came out of the carriage on the way and they had to go to a blacksmith's shop to have the Dolt put in. There is no reason why this matter should have been brought up here at all. No government did wrong in that respect and I would ask the hon. member for West Prince if he could suggest any other way for bringing a man from Georgetown to the Keppoch hospital ? There is no use in exaggerating these things, or trying to mislead the committee, or attempting to create a false impression.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if there were any outbreaks of small-pox or other contagious diseases amongst the immigrants who arrived during the last twelve months ?
The MINISTER OE AGRICULTURE, yes, there were several cases and they were quarantined at the various quarantine stations.
Where were they from V
1 do not know. They were quarantined at Halifax and Victoria, and I think Grosse Isle also. They were in every case dealt with and the disease did not spread.
Where were the immigrants from Y
1 could not say off-hand. We do not investigate where they come from in our quarantine stations.

The reason I asked the hon. minister is that I notice in one of the reports of the American officers who inspect immigrants going through Canada to the United States caustic references to the condition in which some of the immigrants arrived in Canada. I want to know if there is any laxity on our part in the examination of immigrants which would cause such a report by these American officers Y

I do not think the hon. gentleman has quite understood the situation. Of course, we are not responsible for what the steamship companies do in bringing out immigrants. When they arrive in Canada we have them examined for disease and if there is any disease among them, we quarantine them and treat them. The American authorities, I believe, have an arrangement for officers to watch immigrants arriving in Canada and this has been done at the express desire of the transportation companies who want Mr. HUGHES (King's).
to get this travel for their lines. It is done by the immigration officers of the United States, I do not think with any intention or desire to examine as to disease, but to examine as to what they consider proper qualifications of immigrants both as to their financial and mental conditions. The United States have stringent rules as to the landing of immigrants and their rule at United States ports is that ships must carry back rejected immigrants. Of course, if ships landed these immigrants in Canada and they were discovered in Chicago or Detroit as being unsatisfactory, the United States authorities could hardly force the ships to carry them back. They therefore made an arrangement by which their officers go to the port of landing and there deal with these immigrants.
What becomes of those who are rejected ?
The ships have to take them back.
They are not allowed to land in Canada ?

No. We have nothing to do with them at ail. This is an arrangement between the shipping companies and the United States authorities over which we have no control and over which we have no responsibility.
If these immigrants are found unsuitable by an officer of a foreign government they are not permitted to land on Canadian soil and are sent back again. Is that the situation Y
1 believe so. I cannot say positively, but I believe that is what it amounts to. Of course the immigrants they deal with in this way are only those that are booked for the United States.

Charges are made that a great many of these immigrants land in Canada, remain here temporarily, and then cross the boundary so that practically a general surveillance is exercised by these foreign immigration officers over our immigrants Y

No, none whatever. The immigrants that are dealt with are only those that are booked through to United States points, and who declare themselves as intending to go to the United States. Any immigrant f< r Canada is not touched or dealt with by these United States officers.

My hon. friend from King's (Mr. Hughes) who spoke a moment ago said that I had exaggerated the statement I made in connection with small-pox patients being driven from Georgetown to the marine hospital at Keppoch. The hon.

gentleman corroborated every word I said, instead of exaggerating tlie statement I made it as mild as possible. Here was a case of small-pox, a case coming to our shores where an epidemic might have been spread all over Prince Edward Island and the government of this country, or the local government, let that patient be driven through a part of the hon. gentleman's riding of King's, and a part of the riding of East Queen's from Georgetown to a point near Charlottetown, a distance of thirty miles. That man went in that carriage on which there was placed no flag, without anything being provided to notify the people along the line of the route of the fact that a small-pox case was being carried. The hon. gentleman says that the carriage broke down and that they had to go to a blacksmith's shop to repair it. I am not exaggerating the statement at all, and the hon. gentleman has himself confirmed my statement that this patient having the smallpox was driven thirty miles through the province of Prince Edward Island, liable to spread the disease all over the country, and yet the hon. gentleman makes light of it. The public health of our people is of great importance, and every precaution should be taken to safeguard it. When this gentleman gets up here and says I have exaggerated, he says what is not correct.
What would you do with the patient under the circumstances ?
Kill him.

Let me make a further statement. There was some local discussion about this, and the patient stated himself in the newspapers mat he was quite comfortable during the drive, that every precaution was taken, that he had no fault to find with the means to bring him to the hospital where he would [DOT]get the best medical treatment, and the proof of his being well cared for is that he recovered in a short time, and that the disease did not spread.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Last year this same vote was asked for and also a supplementary vote. Will the $110,000 cover the whole service this year or will the minister ask for more ?
I hope that this will be sufficient, but that will depend entirely on the extent of the outbreak of the disease, which I cannot foretell.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In 1895-6, $35,000 was all that was asked for this service but this year three times that amount is to be voted. How is it possible that there could be such an increase in this item ?

In the first place, the work in connection
with the frontier was not in existence at all in 1895-6, and in the second place we had not a small-pox outbreak, and we had not the Yukon to look after. All these additions have caused the increase.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think the real explanation is that the minister had a number of doctors that he wanted to give $100 a month to, in order that they might draw the money and do nothing. I suppose the minister will give us the names of all the doctors that are employed in the department so that we may know where this extra $70,000 went.
I will get that information.
Did we spend the entire $110,000 last year ?
The $110,000 is for the current year, and I am afraid we will have to ask for a supplementary vote.
What was the amount we spent last year ?
And you are asking for $35,000 more.

Yes, and we will have to ask for more still. I regret to say that this expenditure by my department is only a small part of what the people of Canada are to-day paying on account of this small-pox outbreak. If the hon. gentleman will refer to the expenditure by the local and municipal authorities, he will find that probably several million dollars are expended in Canada this year on account of this outbreak of small-pox.

But the damage small-pox may cause has nothing to do with the inspection along the frontier. The minister tells us that there is no danger from the New England states, and mat the only danger is from the Western states. Thirty-five thousand dollars in addition to what we spent last year is a very large amount, when the prospect is that we will not require so much. I think that vote ought to be reduced.

The hon. gentleman does not seem to have followed the discussion. The expenditure along the frontier has been intermittent but constantly increasing, and the prospect seems to be that it will go on. If it does not go on the money will not be spent, but I fear that it is necessary to provide for this contingency, and this year not only will I have to spend $110,000, but I shall have to ask for a considerable amount more to cover the expenditure for the next four months of the current year. A large amount of this money has been spent in the Yukon and in the territories dealing with small-pox

outbreaks, and the kon. gentleman is mistaken in thinking that it has all been expended in watching the frontier.
It seems to me that we are mounting up this vote at a great rate.
We unfortunately are.

The minister tells us that a doctor goes on each train and examines the patients. At what distance from the boundary line does he board the train, and what does he do in the case of travellers who come fx'om infected districts, but who may not have the disease themselves ?

The doctor works as conveniently as he can, and he boards the train at different distances from the frontier according to the location of the stations. Whenever people come from what are called infected districts in the United States, we require them to be vaccinated if they have not been already. The officer examines them as carefully as possible, and if he sees any suspicious cases, he detains them.

What does the hon. gentleman mean by suspicious cases? A traveller coming fi'orn a district where small-pox is prevalent may have signs of the disease, and he may have been vaccinated. Is he refused admission ?
Yes, and is vaccinated.

I have no doubt the hon. gentleman takes due precautions for preventing the importation of disease ; but if the pi'ess can be relied on, we imported a good many small-pox cases from Michigan last summer, and I believe it is pretty prevalent in some of the lumber districts in Canada to-day. It does seem as if some more stringent precautions ought to be taken.

The hon. gentleman understands that there is a period of incubation for this disease during which it is not recognizable ; and of course we cannot expect to keep everybody who comes from the United States in quarantine for fifteen days. That would be an interruption of traffic which people would not submit to. What we do is to vaccinate any who are suspected of disease. Of course, any actual cases which are discovered we stop at once and deal with. I do not think we can do much more ; I do not know what more we can do. That has been the working out of the problem by the Superintendent General of Public Health, and I confess I have not myself been able to suggest any further precautions. I may say that one or two cases have occurred which are supposed to have come from the United States. They are cases in which Hon. Mr. FISHER.
the disease was in incubation and quite unrecognizable ; and we must acknowledge that no quarantine regulations would absolutely shut out such cases when they come into the country overland. If they came across the ocean, we might do so.

I refer to cases which have come in on ti'ains. I was informed last summer by a passenger that many passengers came from districts in Michigan where the disease was prevalent, and they were neither vaccinated nor detained, but were coming into the province with perfect impunity.
Was there a doctor on the train ?
I do not know.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that if an epidemic were brought by a vessel to Prince Edward Island, the local authoi'ities woxxld be charged with the cost of dealing with it. At all events, we have this fact, that this smallpox patient was taken charge of by the local government and was driven through the province for thirty miles without any precaution being taken to prevent the spread of the disease. My hon. friend from King's asked, what would you do in a similar case? The proper course to pursue was this-to have a building in the vicinity of Georgetown, where this patient could be placed and attended to by nurses. They have had another case since, and the patient was placed in the vicinity of Georgetown and attended by nurses, and not driven through the country, as the other one was, it would almost appear for the purpose of spreading this dread disease through the province. I have only stated what I know to be correct, and the hon. member for King's has corroborated the statement I made. I think there must be some difficulty between the government of Prince Edward Island and the government of Canada when smallpox cases can be treated in this way. The hon. gentleman said the man was comfortable when he was driven thirty, miles through the country, and had his carriage broken down. How could he be comfortable, or how could he be expected to r ecover ? I was told that the poor man was so terror-stricken that ho was unable to walk from the carriage to the hospital, and had to be helped. I say that such conduct on the part of the government or on the part of any man is a disgrace and a discredit to our country, and that we should unite to see that humanity, at all events, is extended to people in such a condition.

I took the liberty of making an inquiry of the Minister of Agriculture respecting the steps which had been taken by the United States authorities to examine immigrants arriving in Canada. I had glanced over the report of the United States Commissioner of Immigration for the

past year, and I thought I was justified in asking the question I did from the recollection I had of the statements contained in that report. I have obtained a copy of the report since, and it fully justifies the statement I made. I find at page 32 of the report, under the heading of ' Diseased Immigrants ' the following statement. I will not occupy the time of the committee by reading the statistics of the number of diseased immigrants sent back by the United States. They totalled 309, composed of various nationalities. The report states :
These represent, however, only such as appll-fed for admission to the United States, and the bureau reiterates the opinion heretofore expressed that the vigilant inspection at our ports has resulted, to some extent, in diverting diseased aliens to Canada, whence they surreptitiously effect an entrance across our northern boundary line. An attempt was made to cheek this evil by locating a surgeon of the United States marine hospital service at Liverpool, England, who by the consent of the various steamship lines plying to Canadian ports, was permitted to make a physical examination of the passengers. The experiment, however, proved unsuccessful, as some of the vessels brought diseased aliens who had been rejected by the said officer, and there were no means of deterring any of the said lines from bringing diseased persons to Canada, whose declared purpose to remain there would be no bar to their subsequently crossing the boundary line and coming into this country. That diseased persons who have been rejected at ports of this country do actually effect entrance later, probably through Canada, the bureau has heretofore reported that it had satisfactory evidence.
As a partial check on this practice Dr. Victor G. Heiser, of the marine hospital service, has been stationed with the force of immigration officials at Quebec, and there makes an examination of arriving aliens, though, of course, his report that any alien is diseased does not debar that alien from admission to Canada, although the steamship lines agree to return to the foreign port of embarkation those destined confessedly to the United States who are found to be afflicted with a dangerous contagious disease. This action of the steamship line in any particular instance, it seems hardly necessary to say, is contingent upon the willingness' of the diseased alien to be returned to the port from which he embarked.
Then there is on page 34, under the heading of Immigration Through Canada, a statement showing an increase since the 30tli June, 1897, from 6,542 to 21,647 last year, and the commissioner goes on to observe
While the ratio of increase over the arrivals of aliens through Canada last year is comparatively small, it is to be remembered that the figures above represent only such as state their ultimate destination to be this country ; others, who feel a doubt as to their ability to pass inspection, may, and doubtless do, avail themselves of the advantage of a landing and temporary residence in Canada to effect an entry over the boundary line.
The subject of immigration through Canada is now being considered by the department and the various Canadian transportation interests, with the view to effecting an agreement whereby the evils of the present system may be, if not obviated altogether, at least materially lessened.
That is a most extraordinary statement with regard to the quality and character of the immigrants arriving in Canada to appear in the annual report of the commissioner of the United States. It seems to me extraordinary that an officer of a foreign government should go to Quebec and inspect, not only the immigrants ostensibly for the United States, but all the immigrants on the vessels.
He has no authority to do so.

I take this from the official report of the Commissioner General on Immigration. Surely it is not the practice to bring to Canada immigrants, who would not be admitted into the United States direct because of their physical disability, in order that these immigrants may work their way through this country into the United States ? Should we not have as rigid an inspection of all immigrants as exists on the other side of the line? If they are not fit mentally and physically, they should not be permitted to land here. We should put some barrier in the way of promiscuous immigration. I should like to know whether the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States is justified by the facts in making the statements I have just read. Those who read this report must be very unfavourably impressed ns regards the quality and character of at least some of the immigrants who find their way to Canada, and I would like an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture.
What the bon. gentleman is discussing is an immigration matter and not a quarantine matter.
I am speaking of diseased immigrants.

At New York and Boston and other American ports, there are a quarantine station and an immigration station. In the one the immigrants are dealt with from a quarantine standpoint solely, and in our ports we deal with the immigrants more severely than they are dealt with by the American officials. The diseases referred to in the report the hon. gentleman has just read are not what are called quarantineable or contagious diseases, but are dealt with by the immigration authorities at the immigration stations. I have not the detailed information necessary to satisfy the hon. gentleman on the point he raises, but that is a point which should properly come up when discussing the estimates on immigration, and



will be dealt with by the Minister of the Interior. What I said a few minutes ago was strictly correct, that while this gentleman may make a report to the United States government with regard to immigrants coming to Canada, that report does not prove that the United States officials have any control over such immigrants. It is only a private arrangement allowed by our own immigration authorities, and agreed between the United States immigration department and the transportation line, so as to facilitate the bringing of these people by our lines instead of directly to the United States. The statements as to our Canadian immigrants I do not believe to be well founded, and I am sure my hon. colleague the Minister of the Interior will deal with that matter when his estimates come up. I do not believe for a moment that the character of the immigrants who come to Canada is such as would justify statements such as have been read by my hon. friend.

I am very glad to hear the Minister ot' Agriculture say that the statements contained in this report of the Commissioner General of the United States are not justifiable. It is only fair to Canada that the Minister of the Interior should have an opportunity, when his estimates are under discussion, to make a full reply to the charges contained in this report. I took the liberty two years ago to draw attention to some statements not at all satisfactory, which appeared in the report for the then current year of the United States Commissioner General of Immigration, and I should be very glad to learn from the Minister of the Interior that the same rigid inspection is made of immigrants on this side, which is made of immigrants on the other side, and that the statement that undesirable immigrants are allowed to enter Caif-ada because of lax inspection, is not well founded.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I must ask the hon. minister to allow this item to stand until he brings down a statement showing where this money has gone. Take the Auditor-General's Report, page D-71, and you will find there an explanation of how this expenditure has grown from $35,000 in 1895-90, to $110,000 now. The hon. minister has told us that he spent $75,000 last year, but in the Auditor General's Report you will find that the expenditure was $94,000. He has thus deceived the House by $20,000 in his statement. He asks now $110,000, and says he will have to ask for an additional amount in the supplementaries. In the Auditor General's Report, page D-71, you will find an explanation of this extravagance down in the village of Montmagny. I find that Alphonse Labarge draws $848 for a few supplies. Let me give a few of the items so as to show the outrageous prices charged. I find four kegs of nails at $16.25; eight gallons of linseed oil at $1.10 a gallon; 163 Hon. Mr. FISHER.
pounds of putty at 8 cents a pound; Here is another charge of 163 pounds of putty at 8 cents per pound. You can go to any retail hardware store in the city of Ottawa and buy it at 3 cents a pound. 200 pounds of soft soap is charged at 13 cents per pound. There is another gentleman, Mr. Lesperance, in the same constituency who furnished some supplies. We find, for instance, a ton of coal $8.50; 22 pounds of beef at 22 cents, and 22 pounds of beef at 20 cents; coal oil, 464 gallons at 32 cents a gallon, 306 pounds of sugar at 6J cents per pound. And so it goes, hundreds and hundreds of dollars paid out by this government buying from retail merchants and paying three or four times what they can get the goods for in any respectable store. Any person who has purchased any of these goods must know that the prices named here are, to say the least of it outrageous ? Hut, it is just the same through all the Auditor General's Report. This accounts for the amount of expenditure of this government. They spend here $110,000 on a service that was given in 1896 for $35,000. it is no wonder the expenditure of this country has crept up to $57,000,000, instead of $37,000,000, the amount for which the late government conducted the affairs of the country with as great efficiency or more. Hut there were not so many doctors employed at $100 a month to do nothing.
Carried.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
No, it is not carried. The minister will furnish the statement he promised before the item passes.
.Mr. ROSS (Ontario). I think this discussion has been useful. I know that I have gained information regarding quarantine that I had not even dreamed of. When the minister was reading the list of those employed, I did not hear the names of any officers read out as being appointed at Sarnia, Windsor or Niagara, at which points the trains come over from the United States.

No, we have none there now. I think that for a time last summer officers were appointed at one or more of these places. 1 have promised to give a list of those temporarily employed, but not now employed. When that list is ready it will show the hon. gentleman what has been done at the frontier referred to.

It is generally felt in this country that the state of Michigan is responsible for the small-pox in Canada. In that case, we might expect that the small-pox would come in at Sarnia. To show how the Americans do, I may say that I met a gentleman from our town returning from the west who told me that lie had been going to Michigan, but was stopped at Sarnia and not allowed to go over because he had not bpen vaccinated

within two months. The United States know how to look after the people going into their country. Here was a man perfectly healthy in appearance, but kept out of the state of Michigan, prevented even from going through on the regular line of railway, because he had not been vaccinated within two months. I do not agree with file hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that too much has been spent on quarantine. My fear is that the minister has not asked for enough to guard the country against the terrible scourge o'f small-pox.
Mr. 1AuitAM.	The difficulty does not
seem to be that not enough was asked for, but in the way it is distributed. The province of Ontario, is paying a great dear 10 prevent the spreaii or smali-pox. The matter is in the lianas of the provincial government. But, when we refer to British Columbia we tind large sums paid out by this government to prevent the spread of disease in that province. So far as 1 know, in the past few years they have been troubled a great deal in that province. But, if they forget to look after that matter I do not see why this government should be called upon to pay money for that province if it does not pay for the others. Take, for instance, the case of liossland, in British Columbia. It is a small place and in from the boundary line. Yet, there are two doctors there employed by this government. And other doctors are employed in many cases in British Columbia, ft is unfair that the government should take these measures in one province, and, to a great extent, overlook other provinces.
The MINISTER Oh' AGRICULTURE. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) must noi imagine that the expenditure of the money of this vote in British Columbia has to uo with the interior of that province, ft lias to do with the international boundary line. 1 have already explained that we acted when we knew there was the disease at any point south of the boundary line, and also that we acted on representation being made by the health authorities of the province that it was necessary. In the province of Ontario, it happens, we have been remarkably free from demands, except so far as the traffic between Ontario and Michigan was concerned-and, mainly that with the northern part of the state. We have a number of officers around Sault Ste. Marie and adjacent ports to protect our people. In the state of Washington and Oregon, the position is much worse than it is in the eastern states; and it is for that reason, largely, that we have spent more money- in proportion than in Ontario. As to the two doctors at Rossland, there is a junction just across the boundary line at North Port, and two lines come in and Uossland doctors have to watch them both.
