I understand the hon. minister to say that there is disease in northern' Michigan, but not in southern Michigan. How is it, then, that the papers in Essex county say that small-pox is imported into that county from Michigan ? We see it stated in the local press also that there is small-pox not very far from Detroit-for instance I see it spoken of as existing in the Plymouth district, seventeen or eighteen miles from Detroit. If that is so, it must be the easiest thing in the world to import it with the regular travel across the line. When Canadians seek to go there without being recently vaccinated or under the influence of vaccination at the time, I am told, they are not allowed to cross. We do not seem to be exercising the same strictness against small-pox as the people of Michigan do. But we are told small-pox has been brought across the line not once, but repeatedly, last summer.

At the present time, the municipalities of Windsor, Walkerville and Sandwich are about to apply for a quarantine station. From time to time we have been very much exposed, and these municipalities have acted as a sort of buffer to the whole province. The result is that they have been obliged to spend large sums of money, much in excess of what other municipalities throughout the province are called upon to pay. t think along the line of the discussion tonight it would be a proper thing for the government to establish at that point a suitable quarantine station for the protection not merely of these municipalities but of the whole province.

That seems to verify our contention that the quarantine regulations are so lax that the disease is brought across the line. There are dozens of cases of it in Essex to-day. I saw the statement within the last two days that there are between 100 and 200 cases in the county of Essex.
There are not more than two or three cases in the whole county.
The Ontario government is spending a large amount of money in connection with this quarantine. Are the Ontario government and this government working in harmony or on separate lines ?

They are on separate lines, because the Ontario government's duty is to look after health within the province. Our duty is to look after the frontier alone, we do not undertake to deal with the interior of the provinces. When we have been notified by the provincial health authorities that there seems to be danger of the disease coming across the frontier, we take the necessary steps to protect them.

I would like to call the minister's attention to page D-75 of the Auditor General's report, to the following item : ' Baxter, John, M.D., Thessalon, paid $810.71; Parker, F., M.I)., Bruce Mines, $387.00 ; Aylesworth, G. M., M.D., Colling-wood, $520,000. Now these payments are all in connection with looking after smallpox. May I ask the minister under what rule or system these gentlemen were paid, because these are not frontier towns or villages.

I think Thessalon is one of the lake ports, and I think the other places are too. It was represented that ships were coming in from infected parts in the United States and liable to bring small-pox ; therefor we appointed doctors there.

I am sorry the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Dyrnent) is not in his place. But it does seem odd that a small village like Thessalon should require a doctor to be paid the enormous sum of $810. There no trade at Thessalon beyond an odd vessel coming in for lumber. There is some reason for the services of medical gentlemen at the Soo. There is Dr. Gibson, $1,130, and Dr. Shepherd, $354. I may tell the minister that tlie complaint is current that all the small-pox that has infested the northern part of Ontario has been brought in across the border at Sault St. Marie. The result has been not only a huge expense to the province but to the municipalities as well. There must have been a great deal of laxity at the Sault St. Marie to have permitted so many cases to come in across the border there. What was the result ? Men coming from Michigan went to the lumber camps in that district, and with the breaking up of operations in the spring they proceeded to different parts of the province and thus transplanted these cases for distances of 100 miles. I know in our own neighbourhood, in the town of Midland and in the township of Tay, tlie result lias been the expenditure of hundred of dollars by the municipalities in looking after these cases. I am well within the mark in saying that in the township of Tay there were seven or eight cases imported directly from these districts, and the result has been that the township authorities were compelled to quarantine the people in their houses, to place guards over them to prevent communication with other persons. More than that, they had to provide means and supply provisions for them for a long ^tinie. There must have been a great laxity of surveillance at Sault Ste. Marie not to have prevented so many cases crossing the border. While I regret to bring up this case of Thessalon in the absence of the member for Algoma, it is a striking thing that at a small village like that a medical gentleman should have been paid the huge sum of $810. Dr. Aylesworth of Collingwood was also paid a large
sum, that is in the riding of North Simcoe. For the future I trust the minister will see that better means are taken at Sault Ste. Marie to prevent cases coming across and spreading through the northern part of Ontario. It is not simply a matter of spending money in looking after cases when they had got so bad as they did, but there were many cases where people died. I may mention a case that occurred in the town of Orillia. A man came in from one of those lumber districts and went to a leading hotel in the town, and it was found that he had the small-pox. The result was the closing of the hotel for a long time, and a great loss of money to the proprietor, all in consequence of this small-pox spreading from the Soo eastward and all over that district of northern Ontario.

In my experience I chanced to be in the neighbourhood of tlie Soo about a year ago. There were two cases of small-pox detected on a train, not by a medical health officer of the provincial government, not by a medical man at all, but by some gentleman who happened to be on the train and who was familiar with it. They were in a second class car. The passengers with whom they had been associated, for how long a distance I do not know, were turned loose into the first class car and those in the first class car were run into the sleeper. One can readily imagine the sensation on that train. Those two passengers were finally quarantined in a second class coach at Sudbury and the train moved on. I can assure the minister that there was a very nervous feeling among the passengers, at all events I can speak for a good many of them. They were in doubt as to whether they should voluntarily go into quarantine, or whether they should go and get themselves fixed up by being fumigated, or what other course to pursue. I mention this to show that these two men had small-pox opened out on them and yet they had been roaming round the country and spreading the contagion.
Did they come across from Michigan ?
Certainly.

I do not know whether it is the intention of the government to appoint a travelling inspector of public health, but if they have not one, it would be well to do so. I have not had the pleasure of reading that report.
The report of the Superintendent General of Public Health is in the Departmental Report.
What is his name ?
The Director General of Public Health is Dr. Montizambert, located at Ottawa. He travels around the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: And makes it his business to inquire how the medical authorities are doing their duty.
He does not inquire into what the provincial authorities are doing, they are outside of his purview. He does not interfere with the local authorities.
I am asking about the Dominion officer appointed by this government. He makes a report as to how the provincial authorities are carrying out their duties, I presume.
Yes.

In respect of these two cases, that of Dr. Baxter, of Thessalon, who is paid $810. and the case of Dr. Parker, of Bruce Mines, paid the large sum of $387, what I said as to Thessalon is equally applicable to Bruce Mines. Bruce Mines is not a port of entry for vessels coming from the United States at all. I don't think there is a foot of lumber shipped from that point. There are no saw-mils there. May I ask how these two gentlemen commenced to enter upon their duties ? Was it by the direction of the minister from here upon the complaint of some person, and who was the person that did complain ?

I cannot offhand tell you who it was that complained or what representations were made. It was certainly on the local representations that there was a danger of the arrival of the disease at these ports. I have not in my mind the exact representations that were made.
Since the hon. gentleman has no recollection of the complaints, was it upon the representation of the member for the district ?
Possibly ; I cannot say.
May I ask if In the case of Collingwood it was on the representation of the local member ?
Possibly ; I cannot say.

These are striking coincidences in one or two of these cases. I know that these medical gentlemen are strongly of the same political stripe as the hon. gentlemen who represent these ridings and it seems to me very odd that at a small place like Thessalon this doctor should have commenced on July 1st and continued until the 31st October and that he should have commenced on February 26tli and continued until June 30tli. It is absurd to claim that in the case of Thessalon it was to watch any suspected parties who might come in on boats because it is absurd to believe that boats were plying there at that time of the
year, February 26. In the case of Dr. Parker his time commenced on the 5th of March. No boats possibly could have come in at the time. If the minister has reason to pay these medical gentlemen for services performed there, may I ask him if in the case of these applications which have been made by any of these municipalities he will be disposed to recommend the payment of any of the bills that they have been required to disburse.
I could not make any statement upon such a question until 1 receive representations from these municipalities.
Are these medical officers appointed by the Superintendent General of Public Health ?
They are appointed by him under the minister, of course.
It seems to me that after this discussion-
I am a little in error in saying the appointments are made by the superintendent general. They are made by me as minister through the superintendent general of public health.
He does not recommend the appointments ?
He does not recommend the individual, lie recommends the appointment.
I intended to ask the hon. minister if it is his intention to appoint a travelling inspector under the general superintendent of public health.
I have not any such intention.

I would like to say to the hon. minister that after this discussion, which has brought out some very important information as to the management of his department, we should have some further information. I am in no sense disposed to minimize the importance of a very effective service to prevent the spread of small-pox in Canada, but it would seem, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and also by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Ross), that there has been a great deal of laxity. Now, the hon. minister will see the importance of giving the committee fuller information. The hon. gentleman stated that wherever an appointment was made for the frontier service it was done upon the recommendation of the local health authorities.
No.
Then the hon. minister would say the local member ?
No, I do not say that.

Then I will leave it an open question, whether it be on the recommendation of the local member, upon the recommendation of the local authorities, or upon the recommeudation of some person or persons other than those already stated. It is important that the committee should have that information before them, also the instructions given to persons employed under such circumstances. If the hou. gentleman will permit me, I wish to point out, while we all admit the importance of an effective service, that abuses may grow up under it. The hon. gentleman has stated that many doctors are still in the employ of the government who were originally appointed, while the services of others have ben discontinued. What the committee ought to have in the first place is the information that induced the minister to give the appointment, and in the next instance where there has been a cessation of the service, the reason for Its discontinuance. I think the hon. gentleman had better let the item stand until he gives the committee that information.

Tt is quite impossible, and I do not think it would serve any particular purpose for the director general of public health to go and visit these different localities from time to time. At the time he might visit one there might be no case of disease, and the next day after he left, there might be cases of disease.
The hon. gentleman quite misunderstands me. What I asked of the minister was the information that induced him to make the appointments first ?
I understand that. I was coming to that.

Then, again, what induced him to dispense wTitli the services of those who had been employed. Was it upon the recommeudation of tile superintendent general who made a report to the hon. gentleman before he could act, or upon the report of the local physician employed in the meantime in addition to the report of the superintendent general ? The committee ought to be in possession of that information.

I do not know if I can explain it thoroughly so that the hon. gentleman will understand it. The ground upon which these gentlemen have been appointed is that it has been caused to appear to the director general of public health that there seemed to be a necessity for guarding the frontier at any one particular place. The necessity, or appearance of it, was derived from two things in particular, although other things might enter into it-the first thing, the conditions

prevailing on the other side of the line, and, secondly, the representations of the provincial health officers who had more information in connection with a particular locality than we had. If local or municipal representations were made they were taken into consideration. If representations were made by any well-known individuals in the locality they Were also taken into consideration. But, the appointments were made simply and solely when it was believed by the director general of public health and myself that it was necessary to guard the frontier at these particular places. The physicians who are appointed make monthly reports and the condition of affairs on the other side of the line is carefully watched by the director general. Just as soon as these monthly reports showed that there did not seem to be any further necessity of a doctor's continuance in office and when the condition of affairs on the other side of the line showed that the danger had ceased, this gentleman was notified that his services were no longer required and his appointment and pay ceased. There has been continuous employment of some. In the lake ports during the winter time the danger ceases, no vessels are arriving, and therefore there is no danger of contagion being carried. In other ports which are open all winter there might be danger. This is the system which has been carried out and it seems to me to be the only rational system we could carry out. Of course, if we had at the time immediately the scare occurred-I say * scare,' but I do not mean ' scare ' in a discreditable sense at all-but, when the fear occurred, if we had immediately appointed, on all lines of communication betwen Canada and the United States, a doctor to watch for evidences of the disease, this vote would have had to have been two or three times greater than it is, and it would have involved an unnecessary expenditure if we were to adopt such a system. We have tried by all means possible to keep down this expenditure. I know that the director general of public health has kept as close a watch as possible and with my full approval and under my direction he has always tried to dispense with the services of these officers just as soon as the danger ceased to exist. I can assure the hon. gentleman that has been the instruction given, and I believe it has been most fully carried out by the director general of public health.
Well, every member in this House knows that the inspector general is often helpless against the pressure brought by members and friends of the government.

No.
Mr. CLANCY'. The minister knows very well that is the case, and he need not try

to deny it. It is the tendency under the system of our government, and every one knows that it is the case. The very statement of the minister himself shows that it is necessary that we should have this information.
I will give all the information.
And the item will stand until we get that information ?
I will let it stand if you wish.
I assume there is some correspondence between the federal government and the provincial governments on this matter, and I think we ought to be in possession of that.
That correspondence would be very voluminous.
It is very important.
The hon. gentleman had better move for a return and I will bring it down.
The minister cannot get this item passed without giving this information.
If I am to rend all the correspondence between the director general of public health and the local authorities on this matter, it will take the House several days to listen to me.
If the minister places the correspondence at our disposal he will have the assistance of this side of the House.
I will have to get copies made.
The minister has a staff of officers, and the difficulty of getting copies is not insuperable.

Yes.
The minister told us that we spent $75,000 last year in connection with this service, but as a matter of fact we spent $20,000 more.
That was the figure supplied me by the acting deputy minister, and I took it to be correct.
There was a mistake made.
I will find out where the discrepancy is.

If the minister does that he will do something which is less necessary than what I want him to do. During that |
year we were threatened with small-pox, because in the expenditure of $94,000 there is included the cost of vaccine and patrolling and other items which indicate that we feared an invasion of the disease. The minister tells us that this year we are spending not only that amount and $15,000 more, but also a great deal more than that. In what particulars have that increased expenditure been made. Now, the question put by the hon. gentleman for Toronto (Mr. Osier) is very pertinent. In the province of Quebec when we are threatened with an invasion of small-pox, we attend to it ourselves, a fact which is borne out by the statement of the minister that although there is smallpox in the New England states, he has not been asked to take precautions in regard to the frontier of Quebec, and he has not done so. The frontier of Quebec is guarded, and I assume it is done by the local authorities. But the minister has guarded the frontier of other provinces. This very fact shows that the correspondence with the provincial authorities is necessary. I want to know if the department follows one rule in oue province and another rule in another province.
No.
Then there must be some fixed rule in the department, and we have a right to know what it is before we vote this increased expenditure of $30,000.

I venture to say that the minister cannot tell me how many cases of small-pox have occurred on the frontier during the past month, because so far as I can see from the report of the director general of public health, there is very little reference to that matter. It is not the duty of the department to tell us where the small-pox is located along the frontier. I halve here the Public Health Report of the United States, published according to Act of Congress, and this report shows at a glance the number of cases of small-pox in the frontier states and the date of each case. In Minnesota, for instance, there are 2,676 cases and 12 deaths; in North Dakota, 183 cases and 1 death, and so on. That is a very satisfactory report, and it shows that the authorities in the United States are alive to this important matter, and place before the public the very information which we have tried to get from the minister this evening. If it does cost' the people of the United States money they have something to show for it; but so far as I can find from the report of our department, there is nothing to justify the expenditure that we are making.
The information contained in that report issued by the United States authorities, is obtained from the state authorities. We have not done that.
Why not ?

We have not attempted to do it. That information is published in the reports issued by our provincial authorities, who have charge of such matters within each province. We are only supposed to deal with the importation of the disease across the frontier, and in our report you will find the number of cases that our quarantine officers have dealt with.
I understand the minister to say that in the appointment of these doctors in the Algoma district, he acted on the representations of the member for Algoma (Mr. Dyment).
Speaking from memory, 1 think so.

I think so too, and I think it is rather creditable to the hon. gentleman who represents that district, that he seems to have passed the word to his medical friends-for I assume they are his medical friends-that they had better start at this calling on a certain date; because it is a very odd coincidence that Dr. Baxter of Thessalon, started on his duties on July 1st, and ended them on the 31st of October; that Dr. Hamilton, of Fort William, started on the same date and ended on the same date; that Dr. Gibson, of Sault Ste. Marie, also started on the same date, and ended on the same date. It seems that the word was spread about that these gentlemen might give their services to the government at the very fair salary of ?100 a month. I find also that Dr. Aylesworth, of Colling-wood, started on the 1st of July, and ended on the 31st of October. It is absurd to argue that they were all on the look-out for vessels, because Dr. Parker, of Bruce Mines, started on the 5tli of March, long before navigation opened. I would ask the hon. minister specially to bring down the correspondence which relates to the appointment of these medical gentlemen in the district of Algoma at the points which I have referred to.

I may state for the information of the committee in regard to the health officer at Rondeau, that in some winters the boats run all winter, and in others they only run to the 1st of January. This year they stopped running in Decern-ber, and of course the officer quit work when the boats stopped running.

Did the hon. gentleman recommend the appointment, and was it solely upon his recommendation that Dr McCullough was appointed at that port V Mr. STEPHENS. I did not recommend the appointment at all. I think the appointment was recommended by the Ontario Health Department-by Dr. Bryce.
I think Dr. Bryce has quite as much zeal in a party sense as the hon. gentleman himself.

I have no doubt it was a good appointment, because I understand that he found men who actually had smallpox, and sent them back to Cleveland. On the whole, it strikes me that it would be very hard for any minister to do what the opposition recommends. One man gets up and complains that he is spending altogether too much money, while others recommend that more money should be spent.

I had no iutention of referring to the appointment, which I believe was made on the recommendation of the hon. member for Kent. I prefer to discuss the question on its merits. So far as 1 can learn, there was not a case of small-pox in that quarter ; but I ask the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Johnston), who represents a constituency where people may come across at all times, whether it was not reported on good authority that there were a good many cases of smallpox in Marine City on the River St. Clair. That lion, gentleman, I will say it to his credit, did not load physicians on the public service, although he is a physician himself. My hon. friend from Kent knows perfectly well that the object was simply to take care of Dr. McCullough. I would have preferred to be spared making any reference to the appointment, for which there is no defence whatever. If Dr. Bryce made the recommendation, he had better turn his attention to the frontier along the River St. Clair or to Windsor, which escaped his vigilant eye.

The hon. gentleman has spoken of Rondeau.
I may say that boats run direct to that point from Cleveland, which was one of the places most infested with small-pox. In regard to what the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has said, there is a very simple explanation. The fear of small-pox existed in the month of June, and there was a very general demand for the immediate appointment of health officers. These appointments all commenced about the 1st of July, because that was when the fear arose and the demand was made, and they ceased on the same date, because that was the date when navigation on the lakes ceased.
The hon. me'mber for Both well (Mr. Clancy) tries to make out that the appointment of an officer at Rondeau was all my doing. I say openly and above board that I never recommended it.
I am glad the hon. gentleman repudiates it.

I did not know the government were going to place an officer there until I was told so by the department here. The hon. gentleman knows that Rondeau is seven or eight miles from any town or any medical man. It is far different in that respect from Windsor, where

there are many doctors, sflid also a medical health officer, wTio could prevent any person with small-pox from coming into the country. At Rondeau boats come from Cleveland every day, and on some days there are two or three boats. As soon as the boats start again, if the department does not appoint a man there, I will ask it to do so, because I think it is really necessary.

Does the minister keep himself posted as to the prevalence of small-pox in the large centres along the boarder V
The ailNISTEIt OF AGRICULTURE. The director general of public health does. 1 do not.
air. HUGHES (Victoria). The minister is the Minister of Public Health. There is no need of quibbling.
The ailNISTER OF AGRICULTURE. There is no intention of quibbling.
air. HUGHES (Victoria). What are the steps which the minister takes ?

The director general of public health receives the reports of the local health officers, as I have already stated to the committee.
air. INGRAai. Is there a health officer at Port Stanley, from which a boat runs to Ashtabula, Ohio V
The ailNISTER OF AGRICULTURE. 1 cannot say whether there was an officer there during the summer or not. There is not now.
air. BENNETT. I think the minister's reason why the services of these men in Algoma were discontinued in October is a very poor one, because I am informed that small-pox assumes a worse phase as the weather gets colder, and instead of the boats stopping running on the 31st of October, they often do not stop until November, and sometimes December. I am afraid that the fact is that the pressure on the minister was too great for him to resist, and that after a time the appointments were swelling so much that the gentleman in charge of the department called a halt. However, when the reports come down, they will show who recommended the appointments of all these doctors in Algoma. It appears they were appointed for very different reasons. At some places, where a large vessel called, they were appointed on account of the vessel; in other cases, where there was superior zeal on the part of the doctor in applying for the position and on the part of the member in recommending him, the doctors started their duties before navigation opened at all. When the minister brings down the papers, I hope he will bring down those respecting
the appointment of Dr. Aylesworth, of Collingwood.
Did these officers give certificates or clean bills of health to persons coming on the trains ? What charge per head was made for the certificate ?
There was no charge and no certificate.

Certainly the doctors issued certificates and there was quite a rivalry among them. In some instances, in the absence of the doctor, their wives made out the certificates. The usual charge was a dollar, but finally they got it down to 50 cents each.
I have no knowledge of it.
I think it would be necessary for us to see the reports of these medical appointees.
There are monthly reports from each of them.

I understand the minister to say that I was complaining that the expenditure was too heavy. What I complained of was that we were either spending too little or too much. We are spending too much for a very imperfect service and too little for a very good service. And while we have been spending a very considerable sum, our expenditure is without much effect, because the disease has been imported over and over again from the other side notwithstanding all our precautions. I cannot understand liow so large a number of cases could come in if ordinary precautions had been taken. I do not complain of the expense, but of the laxity of the regulations and the provisions taken to prevent the importation of the disease.
Are the services of these local medical officers dispensed with on the recommendation of the chief medical officer ?
Yes, he reports to me and I authorize him to dispense with their services.
Have any steps been taken by the officers of the department to secure the co-operation of the provincial authorities ?
The work of each is entirely separate. We have not asked them to do our work, nor have they asked us to do theirs.

Is there any correspondence in the department between the two ? It would be very advisable for the Dominion to secure the co-operation of the local authorities in stamping out this disease. In some sections of Ontario it has made considerable ravages, and our urban muni-

cipalities have had to expend large sums. It is utterly impossible to think that if there were co-operation between the Dominion and the provincial officers more satisfactory results would not be obtained. It is unfortunate, notwithstanding the appointments of so many officers along the frontier in Ontario, that such a vast number of cases have been allowed to pass.
The hon. gentleman is exaggerating. We have no such information.

The newspapers say so, and they got their information from the medical authorities very largely, and their reports have been found substantially correct. At any rate, I think that better results would be obtained if the Dominion officers would co-operate with the provincial officers.
Is there any correspondence between the Quebec Board of Health and the hon. gentleman's department on this subject V
There are one or two letters and I will bring them down.
Is there any correspondence with the Public Health Department of Ontario ?

I will bring that down also.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I would ask for the same privilege for Manitoba. I understand that the disease spread considerably in Manitoba on account of the laxity of the service at the boundary in allowing cases from Dakota to cross the line. We have had several cases traced to Dakota.
The MINISTER OF' AGRICULTURE. My inspector denies point blank that anything of the kind occurred.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. There is a general complaint in Manitoba that cases of small-pox were allowed to cross the border. The fact is notorious.
Item allowed to stand.
Tracadie Lazeretto, $5,500.
Has the vote been exhausted ? [DOT]

It is exhausted each year. It is a fixed sum paid the Sisters of Charity to manage the hospital and to pay the doctor's salary, and other expenses.
Public Works Health Act, $4,000.
Has the hon. gentleman appointed a travelling physician, as he stated he intended to do ?
I appointed a travelling inspector, but not a physician. His name is C. A. L. Fisher, of Montreal.
What are his particular qualifications and what are the duties ?
The duties are to inspect the operations of contractors and managers of public works, to see that they carry out the provisions of the Health Act.
Is not that more the work of a physician ?
Not necessarily.
Has it no reference to hygiene V
It has reference to carrying out the provisions of the Act.
What was Mr. Fisher's occupation up to the time of his appointment ?
I think he was a real estate agent in Montreal.

It would seem much more proper to .have appointed a medical man. To look after the sanitary condition of a public work would require the judgment and knowledge of a physician. In many cases an ordinary person could judge, but in others the knowledge of the physician would be necessary.
What Is Mr. Fisher's salary?
Is he paid expenses ?
Travelling expenses, not living expenses.
I suppose this has to do with public works under the authority of the Dominion, not those under provincial authority ?
Quite so.

Has this officer furnished a report ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE, yes, it forms an appendix to the report of the department.
Has he visited the public works during the year ?
Yes, those coming under the Act.
All public works carried on by the government would be under the Act ?
Yes, or those under contract with the Dominion or on which Dominion money is being spent.
If lie finds an unsanitary condition of affairs, would lie be competent to deal with it, not being a medical man ?

Under the Act, tlie manager of the work or the contractor or his representative is obliged to have a physician on the work or within reach. The duty of the inspector is to see that these provisions are carried out. He is not required to act as a physician himself. It was thought that we could get a layman to carry out the provisions of the Act as efficiently and at less expense than by employing a physician. The Act calls for proper accommodation in the way of hospitals, proper medical attendance for employees and so on. The inspector sees to it that these provisions are carried out.

If the inspector found something in an unsanitary condition and referred it to the company's physician, lie would refer it to one whose interest is with the contractors. The contractor will not wish to undertake the expense necessary to change the conditions. How are they to agree upon what is a proper sanitary condition V

There is a sanitary board for each public work under the regulations. This board consists of the physician, the manager, or contractor, or his representative, and the inspector. If there were a serious dispute, the director general of public healtli would be called in. This work is done under his supervision and control, and he would be the professional referee.
I apprehend that the inspector would have but little influence, having against him two men whose interests are those of the contractor.
He can always refer to the director general of public health.	#	.
How many times is it necessary for the inspector to visit these public works ?
Taking up his duties last year, he visited every public work, and he will probably visit them again during the coming year. We get reports from these local boards.

I fear that these reports will not be as valuable as if coming from the inspector, because of the fact that they are from the representative of the contractor, and it would be their object to defend themselves as far as possible.

Of course, there is a penalty upon the contractor if lie does not carry out the regulations, and it is the inspector's duty to see that the law in this respect is lived up to. Of course we cannot have an inspector on
these works all the time, but we can have him go whenever possible. Mr. Fisher went through to the Pacific Coast last year and visited every work.

It seems to me that if the work is to be effective it will be necessary for the inspector to visit each public work from time to time. Premises might be in a sanitary condition to-day then, a month hence, be in the very opposite condition. The object is a good one if properly carried out, it would no doubt have beneficial results for the labouring men who have but little influence in controlling the situation in these matters. But, to carry out the Act effectively it seems to me, an intelligent medical man should be appointed, and he should visit the works every two or three months.

I think it a great pity that the government, when inaugurating the work of this Act, did not choose as inspector a physician. From what I know, of Mr. Fisher, I believe that he is an old man. I have known him as a real estate agent, I believe, and, I think he is one of the principle organizers of the Liberal party.
He was secretary of the Liberal Club.

I think the department made a great mistake in not choosing a young physician. One could have been employed at far less expense than this. The government could have chosen a young physician, one at the beginning of his career, and thus have given him encouragement, which is always welcome at such a time. I cannot understand why we have an expenditure last year of $606 and, with a salary of $1,800 which is far too great for the nominee, we have now an expenditure of $4,000. Is there mention in Mr. Fisher's report of travelling expenses ? There must have been considerable to bring the item up to such a figure.

When this question came up on the first item for this purpose, it was distinctly stated in the House that the appointment should not be given to a physician. The work is being done largely in the interests of the workingmen employed on these public works, and it was thought that there would be far more confidence in the operation of the Act if a professional man were not appointed. So far as the expenditure is concerned, Mr. Fisher's term of office did not commence until quite late in the year, the expenditure for travelling will be considerable, as he has to travel nearly all the time.
Winnipeg and St. Boniface hospitals $4,000.

Last year when this item came before the House, I asked that it be increased, but I find that it still remains at the same figure. I think it is well to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and of the committee to the fact

that these two hospitals are practically doing Dominion work. Most of the members of this committee are aware that we have coming into that province now pretty nearly 50,000 people per year, coming from Europe, from Great Britain and from the United States. We have two hospitals there, the St. Boniface hospital, under the supervision of the Roman Catholic Church, but which is by no means confined to members of that church, it is a general hospital in every particular; then we have the general hospital at Winnipeg. But I want to say that nearly one-tliird of all the patients treated in these, hospitals are immigrants who have arrived either at once or within a year. Now, is it fair to the people of the west that they should be asked to support these hospitals when the balance of Canada gets the benefit ? I think this item should be increased to at least $10,000, and should be distributed equally between the two hospitals. It should be charged, if that can be done, to the Department of Agriculture, if not, then to the Interior Department. I know when the Minister of the Interior comes to lay his estimates before this House, and when the Minister of Finance comes to make his budget speech, they will both boast of the great progress the west is making, of the large number of immigrants coming in; they will both talk in loud tones of the large quantity of wheat being exported from that country, and undoubtedly will talk loudly of the great progress of the west. If that is so, why should they not contribute at least something to help the sick of those people who come to the west to create that wealth ? I think my hon. friend from Provenclier (Mr. LaRiviere) will back me up in saying that the amount voted for these two hospitals is too small, that the Dominion govern-men should pay at least $10,000, to be divided equally between them.
Mr. LaRIVIERB. We had in the estimates in former years the sum of $10,000 for these two institutions. I am sorry it has been decreased, not so much by the present government as by the former one. At any rate, tlie amount is quite inadequate, as my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) said; because these two institutions are performing the duty of taking care of sick people not only for Manitoba but for the Northwest. When immigrants arriving at Winnipeg take sick, as they frequently do after the long sea voyage, they are sent to either one of these two institutions regardless of creed or nationality. They are both general hospitals. In fact, I may say that the St. Boniface hospital, though known to be a Roman Catholic institution, cares for more Protestants than Roman Catholics. I agree with my hon. friend who has just spoken, and join him in begging the government to reconsider their recommendation and to increase the amount which is offered to these two institutions.
